| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN (ip,setkey) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where (like(process,"%xfrm%") OR process_name="setkey") AND (like(process,"%127.0.0.1%") OR like(process,"%::1%")) AND (like(process,"%state add%") OR like(process,"%policy add%") OR like(process,"% add %")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Namespace creation followed by loopback IPsec setup (DirtyClone exploit chain) AIExploitation High
Correlates UC1 and UC2 on the same host: a non-root user creates a user+network namespace and, within minutes, configures an IPsec XFRM tunnel on loopback. The two-step temporal chain is the full DirtyClone (CVE-2026-43503) precondition and is far higher fidelity than either step alone. Rationale: Joins the two article-stated steps (namespace-granted CAP_NET_ADMIN, then loopback IPsec tunnel) within a 10-minute window on one host — the complete DirtyClone setup sequence. Temporal correlation removes the residual FP from rootless-container namespace noise and admin IPsec testing seen individually. Sigma/Datadog left empty: cross-event temporal join is not expressible as a single-event-shape rule. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/dissecting-and-exploiting-linux-lpe-variant-dirtyclone-cve-2026-43503/ • https://ubuntu.com/blog/dirty-frag-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A rootless container runtime that both creates namespaces and programs xfrm for in-cluster encryption on the same node within 10 minutes (rare)
  • Automated IPsec lab/CI that namespaces a test then keys loopback SAs
  • Admin reproducing the DirtyClone PoC for validation
  • Security scanner exploit-check modules running both steps
Response runbook
1) Triage: this chain is high-confidence malicious on a production multi-tenant/CI/K8s host — confirm the user is unprivileged and not a container-runtime service account, and capture both command lines. 2) Contain: immediately isolate/cordon the host, capture volatile memory, and treat root on that machine as compromised — rotate credentials and any secrets cached on it before rebooting (reboot erases the in-memory binary tampering). 3) Hunt: sweep the rest of the cluster/tenant for the same two-step pattern, check kernel version against the CVE-2026-43503 patch (UC4), and review su/sudo/auth logs for anomalous root grants post-event.
let win = 10m;
let ns = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName =~ "unshare"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","-U") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
    | project NsTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, NsUser = AccountName, NsCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("ip","setkey")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "xfrm" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project IpTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, IpUser = AccountName, IpCmd = ProcessCommandLine
| join kind=inner ns on DeviceId
| where IpTime between (NsTime .. NsTime + win)
| project DeviceName, NsUser, IpUser, NsTime, IpTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', IpTime, NsTime), NsCmd, IpCmd
| order by IpTime desc
let win = 10m;
let ns = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where TargetProcessName has "unshare"
    | where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--user","-U") and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("--net","-n")
    | project NsTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, NsUser = ActorUsername, NsCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("ip","setkey")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "xfrm" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","::1")
| project IpTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, IpUser = ActorUsername, IpCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| join kind=inner ns on DvcHostname
| where IpTime between (NsTime .. NsTime + win)
| project DvcHostname, NsUser, IpUser, NsTime, IpTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', IpTime, NsTime), NsCmd, IpCmd
| order by IpTime desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/[/](ip|setkey)$/i | CommandLine=/xfrm/i | CommandLine=/127.0.0.1|::1/ | join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/unshare$/i CommandLine=/--user/i CommandLine=/--net/i}, field=aid, include=[CommandLine, UserName])

| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=unshare OR Processes.process_name=ip OR Processes.process_name=setkey) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.process_name _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval stage=case(process_name="unshare" AND like(process,"%--user%") AND (like(process,"%--net%") OR like(process,"%-n %")),"userns", (like(process,"%xfrm%") OR process_name="setkey") AND (like(process,"%127.0.0.1%") OR like(process,"%::1%")),"ipsec_loopback", true(),"other") | where stage!="other" | stats dc(stage) as stages values(stage) as stages_seen values(process) as cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where stages>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=unshare OR Processes.process_name=ip OR Processes.process_name=setkey) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.process_name _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval stage=case(process_name="unshare" AND like(process,"%--user%") AND (like(process,"%--net%") OR like(process,"%-n %")),"userns", (like(process,"%xfrm%") OR process_name="setkey") AND (like(process,"%127.0.0.1%") OR like(process,"%::1%")),"ipsec_loopback", true(),"other") | where stage!="other" | stats dc(stage) as stages values(stage) as stages_seen values(process) as cmds min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by dest user | where stages>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Hosts exposed to DirtyFrag-class kernel LPE (CVE-2026-43503 and siblings) AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt: enumerate Linux hosts whose kernel is still vulnerable to DirtyClone/DirtyFrag-class flaws (CVE-2026-43503 and the related CVE-2026-43284/43500/46300/31431), i.e. missing the v7.1-rc5 / commit 48f6a5356a33 backport. Prioritises multi-tenant servers, CI runners and container/K8s hosts where untrusted users can create namespaces. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE IDs and patch landmark from the article (fix in v7.1-rc5, commit 48f6a5356a33) plus the corroborated DirtyFrag-class siblings to scope the still-vulnerable fleet. Pure inventory hunt — no behavioural Splunk/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon form, so those are intentionally empty. Cross-checked against Red Hat RHSB-2026-003 and Ubuntu advisory which enumerate the same CVE cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://access.redhat.com/security/vulnerabilities/RHSB-2026-003 • https://ubuntu.com/blog/dirty-frag-linux-vulnerability-fixes-available • https://research.jfrog.com/post/dissecting-and-exploiting-linux-lpe-variant-dirtyclone-cve-2026-43503/
ATT&CKT1068
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Stale TVM scan where the kernel was patched but the device hasn't re-reported
  • Live-patched kernels (kpatch/livepatch) not reflected in version string
  • Containers double-counted against the host kernel they share
  • EOL/isolated appliances flagged but not reachable by untrusted users
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by exposure — multi-tenant, CI runner, container/K8s nodes with unprivileged-userns enabled go first; verify the running kernel actually lacks commit 48f6a5356a33 (not just a stale scan). 2) Contain: where patching can't happen immediately, apply the article's stopgaps — set kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone=0 and/or blacklist esp4/esp6/rxrpc — then schedule the kernel update from stable/LTS. 3) Hunt: on any exposed host, run UC2/UC3 retroactively over 30 days to confirm the loopback-IPsec primitive was never exercised before patching.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Miasma/Shai-Hulud binding.gyp install-time exec spawning Bun stealer AIExploitation High
Hunts the Miasma execution chain where a trojanized npm package's binding.gyp triggers node-gyp during install, launching a JS loader that downloads the legitimate Bun runtime and runs the decrypted stealer (written to /tmp/p<random>.js) under Bun instead of Node. Article-specific because it pairs the binding.gyp parent context with a node/npm/node-gyp -> bun process transition. Rationale: Anchors on the article's documented chain (binding.gyp -> node-gyp -> JS loader -> Bun runtime -> /tmp/p<random>.js), corroborated by JFrog/safedep/Endor; node-spawning-bun during dependency resolution is rare and high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/ • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-hits-leoplatform-20-npm-packages/ • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate native npm modules that genuinely require node-gyp/binding.gyp compilation during install (e.g. bcrypt, sharp, node-sass)
  • Developers intentionally using the Bun runtime as a Node replacement in build scripts
  • CI runners that pre-warm Bun for legitimate test pipelines
  • Monorepo postinstall hooks that shell out to bun for tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("bcrypt","node-sass","sharp","sqlite3") and ProcessCommandLine !matches regex @"(?i)/tmp/p[a-z0-9]+\.js")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the bun.exe launch — confirm the parent is node/node-gyp during an npm install and inspect the script path (/tmp/p<random>.js is malicious). Capture SHA1 and compare to 6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5. 2) Contain: isolate the host, revoke any npm/GitHub PATs and OIDC tokens used on it, and quarantine the offending node_modules tree. 3) Hunt: search the same host/org for the dead-drop markers (UC5), 'Run Copilot' workflow drops (UC3), and outbound GitHub beaconing (UC4).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","node-gyp.exe","npm.exe","npm-cli.js","sh","bash","cmd.exe"))
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("binding.gyp","node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp build") and FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun","node.exe","node"))
    or (FileName in~ ("bun.exe","bun") and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/tmp/p[a-z0-9]+\.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where (TargetProcessName has "bun" and ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","node-gyp","sh","bash"))
    or (ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("binding.gyp","node-gyp rebuild","node-gyp build") and TargetProcessName has_any ("bun","node"))
    or (TargetProcessName has "bun" and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)/tmp/p[a-z0-9]+\.js")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized LeoPlatform/RStreams npm package landing via binding.gyp drop AIDelivery High
Detects the supply-chain landing of the compromised czirker-maintained Leo/RStreams packages by flagging creation of a binding.gyp file inside a node_modules subtree of one of the named malicious packages. The Miasma wave uniquely ships binding.gyp (no package.json lifecycle hook), so a binding.gyp under these specific package dirs is a direct supply-chain compromise indicator. Rationale: Uses the exact compromised package names from the article (leo-*, rstreams-*, serverless-leo, prism-silq, solo-nav, hexo-*) combined with the Miasma-unique binding.gyp drop mechanism, corroborated by safedep/Sonatype as the czirker wave's signature. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-hits-leoplatform-20-npm-packages/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/miasma-returns-leo-platform-compromise-in-npm
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely benign future release of one of these packages that legitimately needs native compilation (verify version against the published malicious list)
  • Internal mirror/proxy caching the package directory during forensic preservation
  • Security researcher detonating a sample in a sandbox that shares telemetry
  • Package name collision where an unrelated internal package reuses a 'leo-' prefix
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the installed version matches the published malicious set (e.g. leo-sdk 6.0.19, leo-aws 2.0.4, rstreams-metrics 2.0.2); inspect the binding.gyp body for the loader stub. 2) Contain: isolate the host/runner, remove the package, purge npm cache, and rotate every credential reachable from that workstation/CI (npm tokens, GitHub PATs/OIDC, AWS keys). 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 (bun execution) on the same host and check your internal registry/lockfiles org-wide for the pinned malicious versions.

Miasma 'Run Copilot' GitHub Actions workflow dropped by node/bun AIInstallation Medium
Detects the Miasma collection stage where the worm writes a malicious workflow (observed as 'Run Copilot') into a repo's .github/workflows directory to scrape CI runner memory for secrets. Differentiator is that the workflow YAML is created/modified by node/bun/npm (the malware) rather than an editor or git, which is anomalous for workflow definitions. Rationale: Targets the article's 'Run Copilot' CI-secret-scraping workflow drop; keying on workflow YAML written by node/bun (not git/editor) is the article-specific anomaly since legitimate workflow edits come from developers or VCS tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/ • https://safedep.io/miasma-worm-hits-leoplatform-20-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1119 T1552.007 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Workflow scaffolding tools (e.g. 'npx', plopjs, hygen) that legitimately generate workflow YAML via node
  • Repo bootstrap scripts that template .github/workflows on project init
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation run locally that rewrites workflow files
  • IaC/codegen pipelines that emit GitHub Actions YAML as build output
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("plop","hygen","yeoman","yo ","create-react-app","renovate")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written workflow YAML and check for a 'Run Copilot' job, runner-memory/secret dumping, or steps that read $GITHUB_TOKEN/secrets context; correlate the writing process to a Miasma npm install. 2) Contain: remove the workflow file, block the push if not yet committed, and rotate all repo/org Actions secrets and OIDC trust. 3) Hunt: search the org for any pushed 'Run Copilot' workflow and for new public repos described 'Alright Lets See If This Works' (exfil sink).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.github\workflows\", "/.github/workflows/")
| where FileName endswith ".yml" or FileName endswith ".yaml"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun","npm.exe","npm-cli.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\.github\workflows\", "/.github/workflows/")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".yml" or TargetFileName endswith ".yaml"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Miasma GitHub dead-drop C2 hourly beaconing from node/bun AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the Miasma/Hades command-and-control pattern of hourly polling of GitHub (commit search for 'firedalazer'/'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom' markers) by a node or bun process. Surfaces non-interactive, regularly-cadenced GitHub API traffic from the runtime that executed the stealer — distinct from a developer's interactive git usage. Rationale: Implements the article's hourly GitHub dead-drop C2 (poll for 'firedalazer' to pull Hades) by counting per-host distinct hour-buckets of GitHub traffic from node/bun — corroborated by OX Security/Endor Labs; process attribution to the runtime separates worm beaconing from interactive git. Cross-checked against: • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/ • https://www.endorlabs.com/learn/malicious-payload-in-ai-sdk-ollama-npm-package
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dependency tooling (npm/renovate/dependabot mirror sync) that legitimately polls GitHub on a schedule from node
  • CI agents fetching releases/tags from GitHub hourly
  • A developer running a long-lived watch/build process that periodically hits the GitHub API
  • Telemetry/analytics SDKs bundled in node apps that report to GitHub Pages or raw.githubusercontent.com
Suppression filter
| where SampleCmd !has_any ("renovate","dependabot","npm install","npm ci","yarn","pnpm")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the node/bun command line and parent chain — confirm it is the Miasma stealer (UC1) and not a known package manager; inspect the actual GitHub API paths for /search/commits queries. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block egress to GitHub from that process, and revoke GitHub PAT/OIDC tokens it could read. 3) Hunt: search the same host for the dead-drop marker strings (UC5) and any retrieved Hades index.js written to temp.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.github.com","github.com","codeload.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun.exe","bun")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), HourBuckets = dcount(bin(Timestamp, 1h)), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| where HourBuckets >= 6   // regular polling across >=6 distinct hours = beaconing cadence (worm polls hourly for 'firedalazer')
| order by HourBuckets desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("api.github.com","github.com","codeload.github.com","raw.githubusercontent.com")
| summarize ConnCount = count(), HourBuckets = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where HourBuckets >= 6   // hourly GitHub dead-drop poll cadence
| order by HourBuckets desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\bun.exe OR */node OR */bun) @DestinationHostname:(*github.com OR *githubusercontent.com)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(api\.github\.com|codeload\.github\.com|raw\.githubusercontent\.com|^github\.com)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|bun)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| count > 6

Shai-Hulud/Miasma unique dead-drop marker strings & payload hash on endpoint AICommand & Control High
High-fidelity catch-all for the campaign's rotating but unique relay markers and the known stealer hash. Matches 'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom', 'firedalazer', the exfil repo description 'Alright Lets See If This Works', the legacy 'IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner' string, or SHA1 6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5 appearing in process command lines / script content. Rationale: Matches the article's verbatim, campaign-unique strings (RevokeAndItGoesKaboom, firedalazer, the 'Alright Lets See If This Works' exfil-repo description, legacy nuke-token marker) plus the pre-extracted stealer SHA1 — these are near-zero-FP IOCs confirmed by StepSecurity and JFrog. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://research.jfrog.com/post/shai-hulud-miasma-alright-lets-see-if-this-works/
ATT&CKT1027.013 T1102.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst pasting these IOC strings into a terminal/script during research
  • An EDR/AV signature update or YARA rule file containing the marker strings being read on disk
  • Blog/article text containing the strings cached locally and opened by a process
  • A SOAR playbook that references the marker strings in its automation code
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe","notepad++.exe","grep","rg.exe","findstr.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("yara","sigma","ioc","threat-intel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match is live malware execution (not analyst research or an IOC list) by checking the host, process lineage, and whether the SHA1 6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5 is present. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately, revoke all GitHub PAT/OIDC tokens, npm publish tokens, AWS keys and Vault creds reachable from it, and search GitHub for repos/commits carrying these markers under your org. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1/UC2 (bun exec + malicious package install) on the same host and across the org's CI fleet, and audit recent package publishes from the affected identities.
union
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","firedalazer","Alright Lets See If This Works","IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner")
        or SHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
        or InitiatingProcessSHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA1 == "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","firedalazer","Alright Lets See If This Works","IfYouInvalidateThisTokenItWillNukeTheComputerOfTheOwner")
    or SHA1 =~ "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:

            - '\Cookies'

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or SHA1 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5") or MD5 in~ ("6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal drop into Startup folder (Turla STOCKSTAY delivery) AIInstallation High
Hunts the specific CVE-2025-8088 exploitation pattern GTIG observed delivering STOCKSTAY: a vulnerable WinRAR/UnRAR extracting an archive that uses an Alternate Data Stream + directory-traversal path to write an executable payload (.lnk/.exe/.dll/.hta) into the per-user Windows Startup folder for auto-execution at next logon. Archive tools should never write into Startup. Rationale: Built on GTIG's confirmed CVE-2025-8088 signature (archive tool + ADS traversal writing an executable into per-user Startup) which multiple second sources (ESET, SOCPrime, ThreatLocker) corroborate as the consistent persistence mechanism for STOCKSTAY/RomCom/Sandworm deliveries; the archive-process + Startup-path + executable-extension triple is high-fidelity because legitimate archive extraction never targets Startup. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/update-winrar-tools-now-romcom-and-others-exploiting-zero-day-vulnerability/ • https://socprime.com/active-threats/cve-2025-8088-critical-winrar-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable apps extracted directly into a user profile that legitimately ship a Startup shortcut (rare)
  • Software-deployment tooling that wraps installers in self-extracting RAR and adds a Startup launcher
  • Admin manually extracting a utility into Startup for a kiosk/shared machine
  • Backup/sync agents re-materialising a previously-existing Startup .lnk via an archive extraction
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file's SHA256 and FolderPath; confirm the parent archive tool and the source .rar (check Downloads/mail-attachment dirs). Detonate or hash-lookup the dropped payload. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Startup artifact, and quarantine the originating RAR; block the file hash org-wide. 3) Hunt: confirm WinRAR version <7.13 across the fleet via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory; sweep for the same SHA256 / Startup-folder writes on other endpoints and for follow-on STOCKSTAY components (websocket-sharp.dll, masqueraded PDF/calculator binaries).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","wzzip.exe")
| where FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".cmd" or FileName endswith ".bat" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".vbs" or FileName endswith ".scr"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","wzzip.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\"
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("lnk","exe","dll","hta","cmd","bat","js","vbs","scr")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
title: WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 Payload Written to Startup Folder
id: 7c2e1d44-9f3b-4a0e-bf21-3a9d5e8c1b40
description: Archive utility (WinRAR/UnRAR) writing an executable file into the Windows Startup folder, consistent with CVE-2025-8088 ADS path-traversal abuse used to deliver Turla STOCKSTAY.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
  - https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/exploiting-critical-winrar-vulnerability
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/26
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\winrar.exe'
      - '\unrar.exe'
      - '\rar.exe'
      - '\7zfm.exe'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '.lnk'
      - '.exe'
      - '.dll'
      - '.hta'
      - '.cmd'
      - '.bat'
      - '.js'
      - '.vbs'
      - '.scr'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_path and selection_ext
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\WinRAR.exe OR *\\winrar.exe OR *\\Rar.exe OR *\\rar.exe OR *\\UnRAR.exe OR *\\unrar.exe OR *\\7zFM.exe OR *\\7zfm.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\\Start?Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\* OR *\\start?menu\\programs\\startup\\*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(winrar|unrar|rar|7zfm)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\Start Menu\\\\Programs\\\\Startup\\\\", field=TargetFileName)
| TargetFileName=/\.(lnk|exe|dll|hta|cmd|bat|js|vbs|scr)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\*" (Filesystem.file_name="*.lnk" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.hta" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.cmd" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.bat" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.js" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.vbs" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.scr") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Malicious .RDP email attachment opened — mstsc launched from mail/download dir (Turla initial access) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the early-2025 STOCKSTAY initial-access vector GTIG documented: a phishing email with a malicious .rdp attachment that, when opened, runs mstsc.exe to connect the victim to actor-controlled RDP infrastructure (a beachhead for deploying STOCKSTAY). Detects mstsc.exe invoked against a .rdp file located in a mail-attachment, download, or temp directory. Rationale: Uses GTIG's documented STOCKSTAY beachhead (phishing email carrying a malicious .rdp attachment that auto-establishes a connection to actor infra); requiring mstsc.exe + a .rdp path inside a mail/download/temp directory excludes routine internal RDP (which references saved .rdp in profile/Documents or no file at all), making attachment-borne .rdp launches high-signal. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1021.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT support emailing a one-off .rdp jump-host file that a user saves to Downloads and double-clicks
  • User downloading a .rdp connection profile from an internal SharePoint/portal into Downloads
  • MSP remote-support tooling that stages an .rdp file in %TEMP% before launch
  • Power user keeping ad-hoc .rdp files in their Downloads folder for convenience
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Documents\", @"\Program Files\") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe") and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"Content.Outlook")))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the .rdp file path and read its 'full address:s:' / 'gatewayhostname' targets; resolve whether the destination is external/actor infrastructure vs a known internal jump host. Pull the originating email (sender, subject, attachment hash). 2) Contain: block the RDP destination IP/host at the firewall, quarantine the source email tenant-wide, and isolate the host if the connection succeeded outbound. 3) Hunt: review DeviceNetworkEvents for mstsc.exe outbound to Public IPs from this and other hosts; sweep for follow-on STOCKSTAY artifacts (websocket-sharp.dll, Startup-folder drops, masqueraded PDF/calculator .NET binaries).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mstsc.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".rdp"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\Content.Outlook\", @"\INetCache\", @"\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Olk\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("outlook.exe","winrar.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mstsc.exe"
| where CommandLine has ".rdp"
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\Content.Outlook\", @"\INetCache\", @"\Olk\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
title: Remote Desktop Client Launched From Malicious .RDP Attachment
id: b4f0a1c9-2d77-4e3a-8c1f-6e9b2a7d3f15
description: mstsc.exe invoked against a .rdp file residing in a mail-attachment, download, or temp directory - consistent with Turla's STOCKSTAY .rdp phishing-attachment initial access.

STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER: mshta from RAR archive reaching internet to pull ZIP from compromised WordPress AIExploitation High
Hunts the RAR-delivered HTA execution chain GTIG attributed to STOCKSTAY: a .rar containing an HTA script runs mshta.exe (the STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER downloader variant), which then retrieves a ZIP of the main STOCKSTAY components from a compromised WordPress site. Pivots on mshta.exe spawned by an archive utility and/or making an outbound connection to a public host. Rationale: Grounded in GTIG's described chain (RAR-with-HTA -> mshta executes STOCKSTAY.MARKETMAKER -> downloads ZIP from a compromised WordPress host); mshta.exe parented by an archive extractor is an inherently abnormal LOLBin lineage, and the Defender variant adds the public-IP egress that captures the WordPress ZIP pull. Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon use the process-tree shape since those schemas lack the parent-on-network field (noted divergence). Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy line-of-business app shipped as a RAR self-extractor that launches an .hta installer
  • Help-desk packaging an HTA utility inside a RAR for distribution
  • Explorer-launched .hta double-clicked by a developer testing legacy HTA tooling
  • Software updater that extracts and runs an HTA configuration wizard
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Windows\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture mshta's command line and the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP it contacted; determine the source .rar and whether a .zip was written to disk afterward. 2) Contain: block the download URL/host (likely a compromised WordPress site), isolate the host, and quarantine the originating RAR/HTA. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by mshta and any child processes; sweep for the downloaded ZIP and extracted STOCKSTAY components (STOCKBROKER/STOCKTRADER, websocket-sharp.dll) and for Startup-folder persistence on the same and adjacent hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","explorer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "mshta.exe"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("winrar.exe","unrar.exe","rar.exe","7zfm.exe","explorer.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

STOCKSTAY websocket-sharp tunneler (STOCKBROKER) loaded by masqueraded .NET process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the STOCKSTAY.STOCKBROKER tunneler component, which establishes the secure-WebSocket C2 using the open-source websocket-sharp library. Surfaces the websocket-sharp.dll being loaded/dropped by a user-writable, masquerading binary (PDF viewer / calculator / stock-market viewer names) — the disguise GTIG says STOCKSTAY adopts. Rationale: Pivots on the named open-source library GTIG explicitly states STOCKSTAY.STOCKBROKER uses (websocket-sharp) combined with STOCKSTAY's documented masquerade (PDF viewer / calculator / stock viewer) and a user-writable load/drop path; websocket-sharp is uncommon in enterprise software, so its presence under AppData/Temp/Public is a strong STOCKSTAY tunneler indicator. Sentinel left empty: no image-load/DLL-load table is available in this tenant's schema. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/stockstay-turla-intelligence-gathering • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party .NET application bundling websocket-sharp.dll and installed under AppData (e.g. some chat/streaming clients)
  • Developer/test machines with .NET projects that reference websocket-sharp in a build/temp output folder
  • Portable open-source tools shipping websocket-sharp from a Public or ProgramData directory
  • Game launchers or IoT companion apps using websocket-sharp for local control channels
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\" and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the loading/dropping process (name, path, SHA256, signer) and check whether it is unsigned and masquerading as a PDF/calculator/stock tool; pull its outbound connections for wss/WebSocket traffic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory, and block the C2 endpoint; quarantine the binary and websocket-sharp.dll. 3) Hunt: correlate to a preceding WinRAR-Startup drop, .rdp attachment, or mshta download; sweep the fleet for the same SHA256 and for the sibling STOCKSTAY components (STOCKMARKET orchestrator, STOCKTRADER) and WM_COPYDATA/IPC-based multi-process clusters.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "websocket-sharp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pdf","calc","stock","viewer","reader")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "websocket-sharp.dll"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pdf","calc","stock","viewer","reader")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: STOCKSTAY websocket-sharp Library Loaded From User-Writable Path
id: 9e1c7b53-4a26-4d8f-bb0a-2f5d6c83e417
description: The open-source websocket-sharp.dll (used by STOCKSTAY.STOCKBROKER for WebSocket C2) loaded by a process in a user-writable directory or with a masquerading PDF/calculator/stock-viewer name.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/google-details-turlas-new-stockstay.html

logsource:

  filter_path:

#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\websocket-sharp\.dll$/i
| regex("(?i)\\\\(AppData|Temp|ProgramData|Users\\\\Public)\\\\", field=TargetFileName)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-8088")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-8088")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-8088")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Photo ZIP campaign targeting hospitality industry delivers Node.js implant for persistent access

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-25 15 use cases 22 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified an active multi-stage intrusion campaign targeting hospitality organizations in Europe and Asia. The campaign uses photo-themed ZIP archives and fake image shortcut files to deliver a persistent Node.js implant and evade detection. The post Photo ZIP campaign targeting hospitality industry delivers Node.js implant for persistent access appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Exploitation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js implant C2 beacon to safedocphoto/recallnine/kentjerk/photodoc-secure .info domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Calendly authentication-laundering phish: 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)' lure to hospitality staff AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound mail whose sender display name is the campaign's exact 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)' string, relayed through Calendly notification infrastructure to launder SPF/DKIM/DMARC before landing on a Cloudflare-gated .cfd download page. Article-specific because the display name, relay domain and .cfd download destination are all named IOCs. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim sender display name 'Booking Manager (via Calendly)' plus the Calendly relay domain and .cfd download page — high-fidelity because legitimate hotels rarely receive booking notices spoofing that exact display name via Calendly's notification system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine Calendly booking notifications forwarded into shared reception mailboxes
  • Legitimate marketing or scheduling tools that set a 'via Calendly' display name
  • Internal staff testing a real Calendly integration
  • Security awareness phishing simulations reusing hospitality lures
Suppression filter
| where SenderMailFromAddress !endswith "@calendly.com" or isnotempty(UrlDomain) and UrlDomain endswith ".cfd"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SenderMailFromAddress vs SenderDisplayName mismatch and pull the EmailUrlInfo URL chain — flag any redirect ending on a *.cfd or freshly-registered domain. 2) Contain: soft-delete/quarantine the message tenant-wide via the NetworkMessageId, block the .cfd domain at the proxy, and warn the recipient reception accounts. 3) Hunt: pivot any clicking user to DeviceFileEvents for photo-<digits>.zip downloads and to the Node.js implant detections (UC3/UC6) on their device within the next 24h.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderDisplayName has "Booking Manager (via Calendly)"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where SenderDisplayName has "Booking Manager (via Calendly)"
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, SenderDisplayName, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, Url, UrlDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Photo ZIP campaign delivery artifacts: IMG-/PHOTO-*.png.lnk and photo-<digits>.zip AIDelivery High
Hunts on-disk creation of the campaign's fake-image shortcuts (IMG-<digits>.png.lnk and PHOTO-<digits>.png.lnk) and the photo-<digits>.zip source archives dropped via browser download. Article-specific because both naming patterns and the 1,989-2,079 byte LNK size are named delivery IOCs. Rationale: Uses the article's two exact filename grammars (IMG-/PHOTO-<digits>.png.lnk, photo-<digits>.zip) plus the documented 1,989-2,079 byte LNK size band — a double-extension .png.lnk written by a browser is almost never benign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/25/photo-zip-campaign-targeting-hospitality-industry-delivers-node-js-implant-persistent-access/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ZIPs literally named photo-<digits>.zip from a real photo-sharing workflow
  • Backup/sync tools renaming .lnk shortcuts in Downloads
  • Forensic/IR tooling extracting samples to disk during analysis
  • User-created shortcuts that coincidentally match (rare — double extension .png.lnk is the discriminator)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("7zfm.exe","winrar.exe") and FileName endswith ".zip")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the .lnk has a double extension and was written by a browser (InitiatingProcessFileName in chrome/msedge/firefox) and that a sibling photo-<digits>.zip exists in Downloads. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the LNK has executed (correlate to powershell.exe child), and quarantine the ZIP+LNK. 3) Hunt: search the same device and account for the Node.js implant path %LOCALAPPDATA%\Nodejs\*.js (UC3) and Add-MpPreference exclusions (UC5).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(IMG|PHOTO)-\d+\.png\.lnk$" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^photo-\d+\.zip$"
| extend SuspectLnkSize = (FileName endswith ".lnk" and FileSize between (1989 .. 2079))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SuspectLnkSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(IMG|PHOTO)-\d+\.png\.lnk$" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^photo-\d+\.zip$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Photo ZIP campaign LNK or ZIP delivery artifact
