Anti-forensic admin password change-and-revert on Cisco SD-WAN Manager AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the operational-security technique Mandiant attributed to this actor: the default/admin password was changed (to enable exfiltration of the SD-WAN fabric config) and then restored to its original value so a logging-in administrator would notice nothing. Surfaces hosts where the admin account password is modified two or more times in a short window. Rationale: Mandiant/GTIG explicitly described the actor changing the admin password to exfiltrate the fabric config then reverting it; two password modifications to the admin account on one appliance inside a short window is the temporal signature of that round-trip. A single change is routine, so the >=2-in-window threshold is the discriminator. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/mandiant-reveals-how-cisco-sd-wan-zero-day-attacks-gained-root-access/
ATT&CKT1098 T1070
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin who fat-fingers a password reset and immediately corrects it
  • Scheduled credential-rotation tooling that updates then reconciles the admin secret
  • Break-glass procedure that sets and then resets the admin password
  • Vendor TAC session temporarily changing then restoring admin credentials
Suppression filter
// scope to the SD-WAN appliances and drop known rotation tooling identities once enumerated, e.g.:
// | where SyslogMessage !has "cron" and SyslogMessage !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the two+ admin password-change events, confirm whether the final value matches the original (revert), and identify the source IP/session performing them. 2) Contain: force an out-of-band admin password reset and certificate revocation, and review for a fabric-config export occurring between the two changes. 3) Hunt: correlate with troot account creation, su-to-troot sessions, evil_tenant.csv import, and any cleanup/validation script execution; verify no config was pushed to edge devices during the window.
let window = 2h;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("password changed", "password updated", "passwd")
| where SyslogMessage has "admin"
| summarize pwChanges = count(), firstChange = min(TimeGenerated), lastChange = max(TimeGenerated), Samples = make_list(SyslogMessage, 5) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, window)
| where pwChanges >= 2   // change + revert within the same 2h bucket = anti-forensic round-trip
| sort by lastChange desc
source:linux.syslog admin ("password changed" OR "password updated" OR passwd)

Rogue SD-WAN control-plane peering from previously-unseen system-IP (auth-bypass / stolen cert) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the initial-access wave Mandiant tied to CVE-2026-20127/CVE-2026-20182 auth-bypass and stolen device certificates: unauthorized control connections (rogue peering) into the SD-WAN fabric from a controller/edge system-IP never observed in the 30-day baseline. Anti-baseline on the peer system-IP parsed from control-connection syslog. Rationale: Mandiant attributed the first/second intrusion waves to rogue peering connections via CVE-2026-20127/20182 auth-bypass or stolen certificates; a control connection from a system-IP absent from the 30-day fabric baseline is the article-specific signature of an unauthorized peer joining the control plane. Lower confidence as it relies on baseline maturity rather than a fixed IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/zero-day-exploitation-cisco-catalyst-sd-wan-manager • https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-sdwan-privesc-4uxFrdzx
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new vEdge/cEdge or controller into the fabric
  • Datacenter migration or controller IP re-addressing
  • DR failover bringing a standby controller online with a new system-IP
  • Lab/staging device briefly joining the production overlay
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the new peer system-IP against the authorized device inventory and certificate serials; if unknown, treat as rogue. 2) Contain: quarantine/deny the peer at the controller, revoke any suspected stolen device certificate, and verify control-plane policy hasn't been altered. 3) Hunt: on devices the rogue peer touched, look for CVE-2026-20245 follow-on (evil_tenant.csv, troot account, su-to-troot, password change-and-revert) and review whether any config was pushed to edge devices.
let lookback = 30d;
let baseline = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(1d))
    | where SyslogMessage has "control connection"
    | extend PeerIP = extract(@"system-ip\s+(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(PeerIP)
    | distinct PeerIP;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "control connection"
| extend PeerIP = extract(@"system-ip\s+(\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(PeerIP)
| join kind=leftanti baseline on PeerIP
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, PeerIP, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub repository. They force-pushed malicious commits and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Compromised simonecorsi/mawesome GitHub Action payload by known hash AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the specific malicious payload pushed to simonecorsi/mawesome during the June 24 2026 tag-poisoning compromise, matched by SHA256/SHA1 on self-hosted GitHub Actions runners monitored by EDR. Fires on file write or process execution of the imposter-commit artifact inside the runner. Rationale: Pivots on the article's three pre-extracted IOCs (SHA256 9f93d77d... and the two SHA1s) which are the imposter-commit payload; a hash match is near-zero-FP, so this is a clean alerting rule for any self-hosted runner that executed a poisoned mawesome tag. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2025/03/18/supply-chain-compromise-third-party-tj-actionschanged-files-cve-2025-30066-and-reviewdogaction
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandboxed runner for analysis
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the file re-scanned generating a benign file event
  • Threat-intel team staging the IOC file on a host for YARA testing
  • Backup/forensic image mounting that re-reads the captured payload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Quarantine\\", "/quarantine/"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner and pull the workflow run that executed it; identify which mawesome tag/SHA was referenced and the repo. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, rotate ALL secrets exposed to that workflow (GITHUB_TOKEN, cloud OIDC roles, registry creds, signing keys) and pin the action to a trusted commit SHA or remove it. 3) HUNT: Search other runners for the same hashes, review egress from the runner during the run window, and check downstream artifacts/packages built by that pipeline for tampering.

Runner.Worker process memory scrape via /proc on self-hosted GitHub Actions runner AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the core mawesome/tj-actions-style payload behaviour: a child process spawned by the GitHub Actions Runner.Worker reading /proc/<pid>/maps or /proc/<pid>/mem to scrape CI/CD secrets from runner memory. Article-specific because it pivots on Runner.Worker as the parent plus the in-image label 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Rationale: Corroborated by Sysdig/Wiz analyses of the identical tj-actions payload which 'identifies the Runner.Worker process, opens its memory mappings and regex-searches for secrets'; the Runner.Worker parent + /proc maps/mem access is the high-fidelity credential-access signal the thin article only labels as 'Runner.Worker Memory Scrape'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1003.007 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Runner self-diagnostic or crash-dump tooling (gcore/dd) reading worker memory during a hang
  • Performance profilers (perf, py-spy) attached to a build process inside CI
  • Custom debugging step in a workflow that intentionally inspects /proc for troubleshooting
  • Container runtime health checks reading /proc/<pid>/status (excluded by maps/mem filter)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("py-spy","perf record","/proc/self/status","/proc/meminfo") )
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full command line of the child process and the workflow YAML that ran; confirm whether a memory-read step was legitimately authored or injected by a third-party action. 2) CONTAIN: Treat every secret available to that job as compromised — rotate tokens/OIDC roles immediately and isolate the runner from further job dispatch. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same Runner.Worker parent across all runners for /proc memory reads, base64-encoded stdout, and any outbound POST to gist.githubusercontent.com or unknown hosts in the same run window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "Runner.Worker"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("maps","mem")
| where FileName in~ ("python3","python","node","perl","ruby","sh","bash","cat","dd","gcore")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has "Runner.Worker"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "/proc/" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("maps","mem")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python3","python","node","perl","ruby","bash","sh","cat","dd","gcore")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

First-seen external egress from GitHub Actions Runner.Worker child process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for CI/CD secret exfiltration: an interpreter or download tool spawned by Runner.Worker making an outbound connection to a public destination never seen from that runner population before. Targets the 'Credential Exfil' stage of the mawesome compromise. Rationale: Sysdig/Wiz note exfil variants that POST scraped secrets to gist.githubusercontent.com or attacker hosts; pivoting on a Runner.Worker child interpreter making a first-seen public connection isolates the exfil step. Sentinel/Datadog left blank because their available network tables in this tenant cannot attribute the connection back to the Runner.Worker parent process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-and-mitigating-the-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066 • https://www.wiz.io/blog/github-action-tj-actions-changed-files-supply-chain-attack-cve-2025-30066
ATT&CKT1567 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate workflow step that curls a public package registry or artifact host (pypi, npm, ghcr) for the first time
  • A build downloading a new dependency or container base image from an unseen CDN
  • Self-hosted runner first run after image rebuild hitting fresh update mirrors
  • Workflow posting results to a legitimate webhook (Slack/Datadog) not previously baselined
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","registry.npmjs.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com","github.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the destination (WHOIS/passive DNS) and the initiating command line — distinguish a known registry/CDN from an anonymous gist, paste, or raw IP. 2) CONTAIN: If the destination is attacker-controlled, isolate the runner, block the IP/domain at egress, and rotate every secret scoped to the job. 3) HUNT: Correlate the connection with a preceding Runner.Worker /proc memory-read event (UC2) and the known payload hash (UC1); review whether secrets were also echoed to the public job log.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

codfish/semantic-release-action GitHub Action has been compromised

StepSecurity
2026-06-25 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 24, 2026, an attacker compromised the codfish/semantic-release-action GitHub repository. At 15:39:06 UTC they force-pushed a malicious commit and repointed several version tags to that commit. As a result, any workflow running against those tags after that time executed the attacker's code inside its GitHub Actions runner.

Malicious index.js dropped into codfish/semantic-release-action runner checkout AIDelivery Medium
Detects the compromised composite action being checked out onto a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner: the malicious commit ships a ~512KB index.js into the action's _actions checkout directory, whereas the legitimate action was Docker-based and only ever contained entrypoint.js + Dockerfile. Any index.js inside a codfish/semantic-release-action path (or matching the payload hash) indicates the hijacked tag was pulled. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact facts: the action was converted Docker→composite and a 512KB index.js was added under the action path (_actions/codfish/semantic-release-action). Legit versions never contained index.js, making path+filename and the payload SHA256 (9f93d77d...) high-fidelity. Corroborated by Aikido's independent write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://github.com/codfish/semantic-release-action/activity
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A downstream fork that legitimately re-bundles the action as a Node/Bun composite with its own index.js
  • Security researchers replaying the malicious commit in a sandbox runner for analysis
  • Internal mirror/cache of GitHub Actions that retains the old malicious artifact after remediation
  • An unrelated action in a different org that happens to share the 'semantic-release-action' substring in its name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("defender", "mssense.exe") and FolderPath !has "\\analysis-sandbox\\"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the FolderPath resolves to a GitHub Actions _actions checkout and the file SHA256 = 9f93d77d...; identify which workflow/repo on this runner referenced codfish/semantic-release-action and which tag (v1.6.1–v2.2.1) it pinned. 2) CONTAIN: Take the self-hosted runner offline, rotate every secret that workflow could touch (GITHUB_TOKEN is auto-expired but rotate any NPM_TOKEN/PAT/cloud OIDC trust), and revoke OIDC sessions. 3) HUNT: Pin the action to the clean v5 SHA across the org, search other runners for the same file/hash, and look for the Bun execution and dead-drop C2 (UCs below) on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has "semantic-release-action" and FileName =~ "index.js")
   or SHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFilePath has "semantic-release-action" and TargetFileName =~ "index.js")
   or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bun runtime executing payload index.js from semantic-release-action path AIInstallation High
Detects the malicious composite action's injected step running the payload via `bun run <action_path>/index.js`. The attacker deliberately chose Bun over Node to evade Node's --require security hooks. A Bun process whose command line references both the codfish/semantic-release-action path and index.js is the execution stage of the compromise. Rationale: Uses the article's exact execution string `bun run ${{ github.action_path }}/index.js` — the path token 'semantic-release-action' + 'index.js' + the Bun binary is unique to this compromise (legit action ran node /action/entrypoint.js in Docker). The Bun choice for --require evasion is called out explicitly in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1195.001 T1480.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate fork of the action repackaged as a Bun composite action
  • Local developer reproducing/debugging the action with Bun on a workstation
  • A CI smoke-test that intentionally executes the action's index.js for regression testing
  • Security tooling detonating the sample in a controlled runner
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Bun command line points at a github.com _actions/codfish/semantic-release-action checkout and capture the parent (Runner.Worker/bash) and the host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, kill the Bun process, and immediately rotate all CI/CD secrets reachable by that job (GITHUB_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, cloud OIDC role trust) — Aikido reports the payload reads Runner.Worker memory to steal secrets in flight. 3) HUNT: On the same host pivot to the dead-drop C2 UC (GitHub commit-search) and to any git pushes/commits the stolen token made to other repos (worm self-propagation).

| where FileName =~ "bun" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun" or ProcessCommandLine has "bun run"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| where TargetProcessName has "bun" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "bun run"

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*semantic-release-action*" Processes.process="*index.js*" (Processes.process_name="bun" OR Processes.process="*bun*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
GitHub dead-drop C2 — commit-search for RevokeAndItGoesKaboom / TheBeautifulSandsOfTime AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the payload's dead-drop C2: it queries the GitHub commit-search API for messages tagged RevokeAndItGoesKaboom (encrypted operator PAT) and TheBeautifulSandsOfTime (RSA-signed eval command). On a TLS-inspecting proxy these unique markers appear verbatim in the request URL; on raw EDR, surface the Bun process resolving/connecting to api.github.com for the same purpose. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim dead-drop identifiers (RevokeAndItGoesKaboom, TheBeautifulSandsOfTime) and the exact search endpoint /search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom — proxy-visible markers are near-zero FP. The Defender/Falcon variants degrade gracefully to 'Bun reaching api.github.com' since HTTPS hides the query string. Datadog/Sigma omitted: no native GitHub/proxy source maps cleanly to the URL-marker logic and it is multi-shape across telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/supply-chain-compromise-codfish-semantic-release-action • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Bun-based tooling that calls the GitHub API during a release (Defender/Falcon variant only)
  • A developer manually searching GitHub commits containing the string 'RevokeAndItGoesKaboom' while researching this incident
  • Threat-intel platforms or scanners crawling GitHub commit search
  • Proxy logging a researcher's reproduction traffic in a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where SrcHostname !has "sandbox" and UserAgent !has "ThreatIntel"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For proxy hits, confirm the URL contains the literal dead-drop marker and the source is a CI runner/Bun host — that is a confirmed C2 callback. For EDR-only hits, verify the Bun process correlates with the index.js execution UC on the same host/time. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the runner, block egress, and revoke/rotate every token the runner held; assume the operator already pulled a stolen PAT via the dead drop. 3) HUNT: Search org-wide GitHub audit logs for commits/pushes made by stolen tokens, new commits matching RevokeAndItGoesKaboom: or TheBeautifulSandsOfTime: in your repos, and the same campaign fingerprint in @antv/graphlib, echarts-for-react, and tanstack-react-router dependencies.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "bun"
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com" or RemoteUrl has "githubusercontent.com"
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
// HTTPS hides the ?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom query string at the network layer; this surfaces Bun talking to GitHub for triage. Use ImWebSession/proxy for the verbatim marker.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("RevokeAndItGoesKaboom","TheBeautifulSandsOfTime","search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| DomainName=/(^|\.)github\.com$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/bun/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*" OR Web.url="*TheBeautifulSandsOfTime*" OR Web.url="*search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*" OR Web.url="*TheBeautifulSandsOfTime*" OR Web.url="*search/commits?q=RevokeAndItGoesKaboom*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`

| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "6b9501e1889cc45c91726729610cf69c2442b8c5", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js npm postinstall dropper: node executing setup.cjs --no-warnings AIInstallation High
Hunts the install-time loader from the @mastra/easy-day-js supply-chain compromise, where the malicious dayjs look-alike's postinstall hook runs 'node setup.cjs --no-warnings', which disables TLS verification, pulls a second stage, spawns it detached and self-deletes. Article-specific because it keys on the exact dropper filename and flag invoked during npm install. Rationale: Keys on the exact dropper invocation 'node setup.cjs --no-warnings' documented by Microsoft Threat Intel and Socket for the easy-day-js loader — a combination that does not occur in normal npm installs. Cross-checked Microsoft + Socket writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://snyk.io/blog/a-forgotten-contributor-account-compromised-the-entire-mastra-npm-package-scope/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal npm package that ships a benign setup.cjs build script (rare, but possible on CI build agents)
  • Developer manually running 'node setup.cjs' for an unrelated project that happens to use that filename
  • CI/CD runner installing internal tooling whose postinstall uses a setup.cjs convention
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm-cli.js","node.exe") and FolderPath startswith "C:\\BuildAgent\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree for the node.exe hit — confirm parent is an npm/install context and look for a sibling detached node child spawning a randomly-named .js from %TEMP%. Check the working dir for node_modules/easy-day-js and grep package-lock for easy-day-js@1.11.22 (SHA256 221c45a7...badf). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node and any PowerShell children, and rotate any crypto-wallet/browser-stored credentials and npm/CI tokens used on that machine. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3/UC4 on the same DeviceId — C2 to 23.254.164.0/24, the NvmProtocal Run key, and protocal.cjs/NodePackages drops.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "setup.cjs" and ProcessCommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where CommandLine has "setup.cjs" and CommandLine has "--no-warnings"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js stealer C2 beacon to Hostwinds 23.254.164.0/24 (ports 8000/443) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the easy-day-js / Sapphire Sleet C2 infrastructure: payload fetch from 23.254.164.92:8000 and HTTPS exfiltration to 23.254.164.123:443, plus the named Hostwinds/onweblive domains. Article-specific because it uses the hardcoded second-source-confirmed C2 IPs and hostnames, not a generic egress pattern. Rationale: 23.254.164.92:8000 (payload) and 23.254.164.123:443 (exfil), plus onweblive/hostwindsdns domains, are hardcoded C2 IOCs confirmed independently by Socket and Microsoft — any internal host reaching them is high-fidelity compromise. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://safedep.io/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different benign tenant happens to lease an adjacent Hostwinds IP in 23.254.164.0/24 after takedown (verify the exact /32s 23.254.164.92 and .123)
  • Security researcher / sandbox detonating the sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively probing the C2 for tracking
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is node.exe / powershell.exe (not a browser) and capture the exact remote IP+port — 23.254.164.92:8000 = stage-2 pull, 23.254.164.123:443 = data exfil. Note timestamp for scoping. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.0/24 at the egress firewall, isolate the host, and treat any data sent to .123:443 as exfiltrated — force-rotate wallet seeds, browser-saved creds and tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for the same /24, then pivot to UC1 (setup.cjs), UC3 (NvmProtocal), UC4 (protocal.cjs) to find the install root cause.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("teams.onweblive.org","maskasd.com","onweblive.org","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DstDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc

easy-day-js Windows persistence: Run key 'NvmProtocal' / protocal.cjs autostart AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage implant's Windows persistence — an HKCU Run value named 'NvmProtocal' (and the scdev service / com.nvm.protocal artifacts) launching protocal.cjs from a NodePackages directory. Article-specific because it pins on the malware's unique autostart value name and implant filename rather than generic Run-key writes. Rationale: The autostart value name 'NvmProtocal' and implant name 'protocal.cjs' (deliberate misspellings) plus the 'NodePackages' drop dir are unique implant strings confirmed by Microsoft and Socket — near-zero legitimate collision. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate NVM (Node Version Manager) install writing a Run entry — but those use 'nvm'/'nvm-windows', not the misspelled 'NvmProtocal'
  • Sysadmin scripting a custom autostart that coincidentally references a NodePackages path
  • Security tooling restoring/quarantining the registry value (will show defender/AV as initiating process)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and RegistryValueData !has "\\nvm\\nvm.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full RegistryValueData — it should point at protocal.cjs under a NodePackages dir; capture the InitiatingProcess (expect node.exe/powershell.exe). Check for the scdev service and C:\ProgramData\system.bat alongside it. 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the NvmProtocal value + scdev service + protocal.cjs implant, kill the running implant process. 3) Hunt: search org-wide for the same value name and for the cross-platform variants (com.nvm.protocal.plist on macOS, nvmconf.service on Linux) via UC4; trace back to the install via UC1.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValueName =~ "NvmProtocal")
   or RegistryValueData has_any ("protocal.cjs","NodePackages","com.nvm.protocal")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run" and RegistryValue =~ "NvmProtocal")
   or RegistryValueData has_any ("protocal.cjs","NodePackages","com.nvm.protocal")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: easy-day-js implant persistence Run key 'NvmProtocal'

easy-day-js implant artifacts dropped: protocal.cjs / NodePackages / cross-OS persistence files AIInstallation High
Hunts on-disk artifacts of the easy-day-js second stage across Windows, macOS and Linux: the implant 'protocal.cjs', the NodePackages drop directory, the loader marker files .pkg_history/.pkg_logs, and the OS-specific persistence units com.nvm.protocal.plist and nvmconf.service. Article-specific because every filename is a unique, second-source-confirmed implant artifact. Rationale: protocal.cjs, com.nvm.protocal.plist, nvmconf.service, NodePackages and the .pkg_history/.pkg_logs markers are unique implant/loader filenames confirmed by Microsoft and Socket — a file write of any is high-confidence compromise across Windows/macOS/Linux. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/postinstall-payload-inside-mastra-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/mastra-npm-packages-compromised • https://safedep.io/mastra-npm-scope-takeover-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1543.002 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign internal tool legitimately named 'NodePackages' as a directory (verify it isn't dropping protocal.cjs)
  • Backup/EDR quarantine software copying the artifacts into a vault path (initiating process will be the security tool)
  • A developer's own .plist/.service file that coincidentally matches — confirm the com.nvm.protocal / nvmconf naming exactly
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","sense.exe","backup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process is node.exe/powershell.exe and the file is the implant (hash protocal.cjs vs 50eae63d...edd65). Note which persistence unit was written to map the OS. 2) Contain: isolate the host, remove protocal.cjs and the persistence unit (Run key / plist / systemd), kill the detached implant, and revoke wallet + browser-stored credentials. 3) Hunt: org-wide sweep for these filenames and the NodePackages dir, then correlate to UC1 (setup.cjs install) and UC2 (C2 to 23.254.164.0/24) on the same hosts to bound the campaign.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("protocal.cjs","nvmconf.service","com.nvm.protocal.plist",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
   or FolderPath has "NodePackages"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("protocal.cjs","nvmconf.service","com.nvm.protocal.plist",".pkg_history",".pkg_logs")
   or TargetFilePath has "NodePackages"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

status: experimental

Exploitation. Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Bun runtime executing codfish/semantic-release-action index.js payload on CI runner · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match

Bun runtime executing codfish/semantic-release-action index.js payload on CI runner AIInstallation High
Hunts the Miasma composite-action payload step on a GitHub Actions runner: the bun runtime invoked as 'bun run $GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/index.js' where the action path resolves to codfish/semantic-release-action. The legitimate v1 action was Docker-based (entrypoint.js) and never used bun, so bun executing index.js from this action's path is the compromise itself. Rationale: Anchors on bun + 'index.js' + 'semantic-release-action' from the article's verbatim composite-action step ('bun run $GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/index.js'); GITHUB_ACTION_PATH expands to the _actions/codfish/semantic-release-action path so both tokens co-occur in the cmdline. The original Docker action never used bun, making this combination malicious by construction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://x.com/step_security/status/2069831503471882383 • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer locally testing bun against a project that happens to have a file named index.js inside a directory named semantic-release-action
  • An internal fork/mirror of the action legitimately re-tooled to use bun for builds
  • Security researchers detonating the IOC in a sandboxed CI runner
  • A monorepo with an unrelated package literally named 'semantic-release-action' built with bun
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain — confirm parent is a GitHub Actions runner (Runner.Worker/bash) and the action path resolves to codfish/semantic-release-action; capture the runner host and the repo/workflow that triggered it. 2) Contain: cancel/disable the affected workflow, rotate every secret that workflow could touch (GITHUB_TOKEN is auto-scoped but rotate any NPM_TOKEN / PAT / cloud creds), and pin the action to a known-clean SHA (v1.0.0–v1.10.0 or v2.0.0). 3) Hunt: search all repos for references to codfish/semantic-release-action@v2–v5, look for the index.js SHA256 (UC2) and bun→api.github.com egress (UC3) on the same runner, and review npm publish logs for unauthorized releases.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("bun","bun.exe")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "index.js"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Miasma index.js payload hash present on CI runner (codfish action) AIDelivery High
Definitive IOC sweep for the byte-identical malicious index.js payload (sha256 9f93d77d...) dropped by the compromised codfish/semantic-release-action across DeviceFileEvents, DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceImageLoadEvents. Any host carrying this hash has pulled the trojanised action. Rationale: Uses the article's confirmed payload IOC (sha256 9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015, byte-identical across both malicious commits). A hash match is unambiguous, hence alerting. Sigma/Splunk/Datadog/Falcon left empty because file-write events on those stacks (Sysmon EID 11, CIM Endpoint.Filesystem, Falcon FileWritten) do not carry a SHA256 for a non-executed script file — the hash IOC only lives cleanly in Defender/ASIM file telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://snyk.io/blog/miasma-supply-chain-attack-malicious-code-redhat-cloud-services-npm-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel analyst intentionally storing the IOC sample on a workstation for analysis
  • An AV/EDR quarantine copy of the file retaining the original hash
  • A sandbox/detonation host where the sample was deliberately staged
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a CI runner and identify which workflow/repo pulled it; the InitiatingProcess shows whether bun executed it. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, kill the bun process tree, and rotate all secrets exposed to any workflow that ran on that runner (GITHUB_TOKEN scope, NPM_TOKEN with publish rights, cloud/CI PATs). 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo referencing codfish/semantic-release-action@v2/v2.2.1/v3*/v4*/v5*, repin to clean v1.x or v2.0.0, and check npm/registry audit logs for unexpected package publishes.
union DeviceFileEvents, DeviceProcessEvents, DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Bun process reaching GitHub commit-search API — Miasma dead-drop C2 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Miasma infrastructure-less C2: the bun-run payload polls GitHub's public commit-search API (api.github.com) for marker-tagged commits whose body it passes to eval(). Outbound to GitHub initiated specifically by the bun runtime (the 'Cleanup Action' step) is the dead-drop resolver beacon, distinct from normal git/node CI traffic. Rationale: Anchors on the article's described C2 design (Miasma polls GitHub's public commit-search API and eval()s the matching commit body) plus the bun-run payload step; corroborated by The Register/SafeDep on the leaked toolkit. Scoping egress to bun (not git/node/curl) and the action cmdline separates the dead-drop beacon from normal CI traffic to GitHub. Sentinel left empty because no process-attributed egress table is available in this tenant (ASIM ImNetworkSession/ImWebSession lack initiating-process), so the bun-specific pivot needs Defender DeviceNetworkEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets • https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074 • https://safedep.io/inside-the-miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate bun-based CI step that genuinely calls the GitHub API (e.g. bun-native release tooling fetching releases)
  • A self-hosted runner where bun is the standard JS runtime and hits api.github.com for package metadata
  • DNS telemetry attributing the resolution to bun when a child git subprocess actually made the call
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the bun process that made the request was launched from the codfish/semantic-release-action path (correlate with UC1) and pull the resolved IP plus any url query if captured. 2) Contain: isolate the runner, block egress from runner subnets to api.github.com for non-allowlisted processes, and rotate secrets exposed to workflows on that runner. 3) Hunt: capture the bun process memory/handles for evidence of Runner.Worker access (secret theft), look for the index.js hash (UC2) on the host, and review GitHub commit-search-API access patterns from other runners for the same dead-drop behaviour.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "index.js" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("bun","bun.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has "github.com"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "index.js" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "semantic-release-action"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime DNS Query to GitHub API (Miasma Dead-Drop C2)
id: b8e1d57c-3a92-4c0e-9f6d-71a4e2c8b903
description: Detects the bun runtime resolving github.com, consistent with the Miasma payload polling the GitHub commit-search API as an infrastructure-less dead-drop resolver.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/compromised-github-action-codfish-steals-secrets
  - https://www.theregister.com/cyber-crime/2026/06/09/miasma-supply-chain-attack-toolkit-goes-public-on-github/5253074
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/25
tags:
  - attack.t1102.001
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '/bun'
    QueryName|contains: 'github.com'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\bun.exe OR */bun OR *\BUN.EXE) @DestinationHostname:*github.com*
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/github\.com$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\/bun(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="bun" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bun.exe") (All_Traffic.dest="*github.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*github.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name="bun" OR All_Traffic.process_name="bun.exe") (All_Traffic.dest="*github.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*github.com*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium

Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Browser Extension Installation via Registry
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0a
status: experimental
description: |

    administrative install of an extension. Often used by adware /

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or SHA1 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a") or MD5 in~ ("9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f93d77d32833a515bc406c46da477142bb1ac2babeecb6aa42f98669a6db015", "5792aba0e2180b9b80b77644370a6889d5817456", "bcb6b1d409144318e8fad2171d6fe06d02299d1a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
